morning.title: Why are Indian companies rushing to tap the bond market?
morning.text: Mumbai: Indian companies are taking advantage of the prevailing surplus liquidity conditions and are continuing to tap the bond market despite higher yields and an uncertain rate outlook, corporate bond experts said.Several large issuers raised funds in recent days and more are expected to come to the market next week, ahead of a potential rate hike and expectations of tighter liquidity conditions. The six-member Monetary Policy Committee will meet October 5-7 amid expectation of a quarter-percentage-point hike in the policy rate to 5.50%.Indian companies are expected to raise more than ₹1,000 crore this week, with Edelweiss Financial Services the first to hit the market with a ₹300 crore non-convertible debenture issue on Monday. Bajaj Auto Credit and IndiaFirst Life Insurance Company are likely to raise ₹250 crore and ₹200 crore, respectively.Read more: JioBlackRock CIO Rishi Kohli decodes Nifty’s inflection point after two years of weak returnsVedanta's board approved a ₹3,500 crore bond issuance, while state-owned Power Grid Corporation's board cleared a ₹5,000 crore bond proposal, according to BSE filings."I do not expect the corporate bond market to slow materially despite the increasing probability of higher interest rates. In fact, there is a visible change in the issuer behaviour. Several large issuers have been active and they are increasingly looking to lock in funding before system liquidity drains out and borrowing costs move higher," said Venkatakrishnan Srinivasan, managing partner at Rockfort Fincap, a debt advisory firm.Read more: Will Nifty extend gains to 4th session on Monday? US sanctions on Russia among factors to decide D-Street actionBanking system liquidity has stood at a large surplus this month because of inflows from the FCNR(B) deposits that banks raised under a central bank programme. The daily average surplus was ₹9.97 lakh crore, compared with ₹3.67 lakh crore in August and ₹1.07 in July, RBI data showed. The sharp increase in surplus liquidity has left banks looking for avenues to deploy these funds, and corporate bond issuances are emerging as one such avenue, experts said.Reliance Industries raised ₹12,500 crore through five-year bonds last week, while Bajaj Finance and Tata Capital recently tapped the market with three-year issuances. The three- to five-year segment is seeing strong demand, as banks have surplus funds from the FCNR(B) deposits, which have largely come in with a similar maturity profile.

morning.title: Shahed-136 Clone Found By Florida Fisherman, Eglin AFB Admits It Lost A Drone
morning.text:
A Florida fishing charter boat made a very unusual catch Saturday while operating near Eglin Air Force Base. Located in the western end of the Florida Panhandle, Eglin is home of the U.S. Air Force weapons test wing. Hot Spots Charters pulled a delta-wing aerial drone out of the water during an excursion, according local charter captain Charlie Green. The recovered drone closely resembles a clone of the Iranian Shahed-136 one-way attack weapon, specifically the U.S. military’s Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS) that took center stage during its first combat use in Operation Epic Fury. The target version of that drone is built by SpecktreWorks and is designated the FLM-136. It was originally designed for mimicking one-way attack munitions, specifically the Shahed-136, which it was reverse engineered from, for testing and training before it was weaponized into LUCAS.

An Eglin AFB spokesperson told us the installation recently lost a drone, but would not confirm it was the same one found by Hot Spots Charters.

“I can confirm that we were doing a test and the test article went down,” the spokesperson told us, declining to provide further details about what kind of drone, when it was lost or the location it went down. They referred us to the Pentagon, which could not immediately provide any additional details. 

“The drone was found by local charter Capt. Daniel Arsenault with Hot Spots Charters,” said Green, who is also an aviation photographer whose work can be found at Aquatic Charlie on social media. “He saw the object at a distance and went over to check it out. When he did, he pulled a good size mahi-mahi out from underneath it, complementing his already stocked cooler full of fish from that morning charter. His passengers helped him haul it aboard.”

“Arsenault and his charter company did all the due diligence possible to notify local agencies of the recovery- and was eventually collected by one of them,” Green added. He did not know which agency.

Images taken of the drone shared with us by Green show that it did not have the engine, propeller or the nose cone/seeker intact. Losing these kind of components is common for impacts into water.

While the Eglin spokesperson offered scant details, the host unit at the installation is the 96th Test Wing, which is the “test and evaluation center for Air Force air-delivered weapons, navigation and guidance systems, command and control systems, and Air Force Special Operations Command systems,” according to the wing’s homepage. It oversees the massive Eglin Gulf Test Range, which “provides approximately 120,000 square miles of overwater airspace, covering the eastern third of the Gulf of Mexico from the Florida panhandle to the Florida Keys. The land range covers 724 square miles and contains 70 specific test and training areas, including an approved depleted uranium test range and the only qualified air-to-ground supersonic range east of the Mississippi River.”

As noted in the opening of this article, the LUCAS drone was used for the first time in combat during the opening day of the Operation Epic Fury war on Iran on Feb. 28. 

“Costing approximately $35,000 per platform, LUCAS is a low-cost, scalable system that provides cutting-edge capabilities at a fraction of the cost of traditional long-range U.S. systems that can deliver similar effects,” Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins, a CENTCOM spokesperson, told TWZ when the command stood up Task Force Scorpion Strike (TFSS), the military’s first one-way attack drone unit, back in December. “The drone system has an extensive range and the ability to operate beyond line of sight, providing significant capability across CENTCOM’s vast operating area.”

“LUCAS drones deployed by CENTCOM have an extensive range and are designed to operate autonomously,” CENTCOM added in a press release. “They can be launched with different mechanisms to include catapults, rocket-assisted takeoff, and mobile ground and vehicle systems.”

TFSS falls under the auspices of U.S. Special Operations Command Central (SOCCENT), which oversees U.S. special operations activities across the Middle East.

While we aren’t sure if the drone found by Hot Spots Charters is the one lost by Eglin, it wouldn’t be the first time something like this has happened in Florida. For example, in 2021, beachcombers in Florida’s Palm Beach County found a U.S. Air Force BQM-167A high-performance target drone that washed ashore.

Indeed, the Air Force has a handful of 120-foot boats, the only vessels in its service, to help recover drones after they are shot down during live-fire exercises, or otherwise need to be recovered from these waters. The boats are operated by a contracted crew from Florida Offshore and retrieve around 100 of the drones each year.

The FLM-136’s origins as a target drone are highly relevant here. Counter-unmanned aerial system (C-UAS) capabilities are being hotly pursued on all fronts across the U.S. military as the threat from them has ballooned. During the war in Ukraine and multiple engagements with Iran, including Operation Epic Fury, one-way attack drones have proven to be a massive threat that is heavily influencing how wars are fought. As far as Eglin AFB goes, maybe the most high-profile C-UAS development as of late that has emerged from there has been arming USAF fighters with FALCO APKWS laser-guided rockets to shoot down exactly the same kind of threat that the FLM-136 is meant to emulate. This program began in 2019, which TWZ was first to report on, but was finally rushed into service years later as the standoff with Iran went hot. Now there are many other programs aimed at dealing with these same threats, including a more capable “fire and forget” air-to-air APKWS.

LUCAS development is continuing at a high-pace, with its ability to swarm cooperatively with other LUCAS drones — a feature we reported as central to the LUCAS vision when the existence of the program was disclosed — being worked on now. You can read more about this here. These systems need sanitized airspace for development activities, and the vast ranges over the gulf are some of the best in the country for it.

So, it’s not surprising to see an FLM-136 floating in the waters off Eglin AFB. Even in the war with Iran, there were multiple losses of LUCAS drones where they were found intact. These weapons are produced to be risked in large numbers, and some failing, for whatever reason, is just part of the calculus.

We will update this story with any additional details we can find about this drone. Though we don’t yet know for sure where it came from, one thing is for certain, the folks on the Hot Spots Charters boat that found it will always have a good tale about the one that didn’t get away.

Contact the author: howard@twz.com

morning.title: SP Group backs Tata Sons listing
morning.text: Mumbai: The Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group is backing a Tata Sons listing after a proposed 2.5% stake sale to monetise part of its holding was delayed, people familiar with the matter said. The SP Group, which owns about 18.37% of Tata Sons, had discussed the sale with Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, with a tax-efficient structure involving a bank or financial institution being explored.The proposal stalled at Tata Sons and was formally taken to board only after the RBI's directive brought a listing requirement into focus, the people said.Also Read: Tata’s rival camps lawyer up ahead of looming legal battleThe discussions focused on a limited stake sale rather than an immediate broader monetisation and the proposal envisaged cash proceeds being paid to the SP Group over a defined period, potentially allowing Tata Sons to avoid a listing, the people said. SP Group and Tata Trusts did not comment.The last discussion on the matter with Tata Sons involved Noel Tata suggesting that separate teams from both sides be created to examine the monetisation proposal, the people said. The monetisation plan discussed earlier was being handled by Farokh Subedar on behalf of Tata Trusts, Ankur Verma representing Tata Sons, and a representative from the SP Group, sources said.Also Read: Tata Trusts says Chandrasekaran reappointment resolution was invalid, rejects casting-vote argumentSP Group chairman Shapoor Mistry had publicly backed the listing and said he looked forward to working constructively with Tata Sons on way forward.The SP Group's backing of a listing now gives the conglomerate another potential route to monetise its stake. A public listing could provide a market-based valuation for its holding and make it easier to attract an investor for part of the stake before an IPO, experts said."The SP Group holds just over 18% of Tata Sons and its intent has been to monetise part of this holding in some form," said Ketan Dalal, founder of Katalyst Advisors. "With the IPO now seeming very likely, monetising through an OFS or post IPO, of course, is one possibility." Post-listing lock-in requirements would need to be considered, he said. "Pricing issues would play an important part, both from the investor point of view and from the SP Group point of view. In any case, it is not a situation of one or the other, but it could be a combination of both routes," Dalal said.An earlier proposal in July involved a share swap under which SP Group would receive shares in a basket of listed Tata companies in exchange for part of its Tata Sons holding. Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran had announced in early August that he would not seek reappointment when his term ended in February 2027 and did not participate in subsequent discussions.But he reversed his exit decision and agreed to continue as executive chairman of Tata Sons for another five years after Tata Sons board approved his reappointment on September 17.The SP Group's Tata Sons stake is held through Sterling Investments Corp and Cyrus Investments and has been pledged against borrowings. The group completed a ₹21,500 crore refinancing in July after telling investors it planned to monetise part of its Tata Sons holding through a listing or share sale within 18 months. It faces a repayment obligation of about ₹3,500 crore by the end of September.

morning.title: JSW Defence Puts V-BAT UAV Through Dronathon 2026
morning.text:
JSW Defence displayed the V-BAT UAV at the Indian Air Force’s Dronathon 2026, an event that put the US-made and India-bound V-BAT UAV in the spotlight. JSW Defence invited senior IAF officials, including the IAF’s Vice Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, and the IAF inquired about the V-BAT’s potential and application.
Dronathon 2026, held at the Pokhran Field Firing Range in Jaisalmer from September 14-16, was an operational evaluation exercise of sorts. Surveillance and reconnaissance, autonomy, swarming, and electronic warfare were among the themes of the event. The V-BAT is a Group 3, fixed-wing, vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) UAV developed by Shield AI, which makes it unique. The V-BAT employs a ducted fan propulsion system that enables it to take off and land vertically and transition to a fixed-wing aircraft, allowing for a longer range.
Shield AI provides an endurance of more than 12 hours, a gross take-off weight of 75 kg or more, and a payload of up to 18.1 kg for the V-BAT, which uses a heavy fuel engine. According to the company, it is also capable of operating in confined spaces, including on the decks of ships. JSW Defence and Shield AI, the parent company of V-BAT, inked a strategic partnership agreement in 2024 to indigenise and manufacture the UAV in India.
JSW has earmarked an investment of $90 million for the business, including manufacturing, assembly, testing, training, and building a local supply chain. JSW and Shield AI have stated that the facility is not just for meeting the needs of the IAF but also potentially for becoming a global centre of excellence for UAVs. V-BAT can be positioned closer to the line of contact to give electro-optical/infrared surveillance, spotting, and tracking capabilities to commanders, according to Shield AI.
It is also designed to operate in GPS-denied and communication-jammed environments, the company added. The IAF’s choice of Pokhran as the venue for live demo of V-BAT makes it clear that the service is looking to evaluate the technology for actual use rather than mere display.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

morning.title: PNS Hunain Damage Image Surfaces After Collision with Indian Warship
morning.text:
Photos that supposedly show damage to the PNS Hunain started making the rounds on Indian defense-focused social media accounts after reports came out about a collision between the Pakistani vessel and an Indian Navy warship in the North Arabian Sea on September 15. These images seem to show serious damage along one side of the ship, but no one’s confirmed if they’re real or where they actually came from.
Right now, these photos are just alleged evidence—they don’t prove what happened during that supposed collision on September 15. If you look at them, you see a grey naval ship from above, with a long stretch of hull that looks scraped up, bent, and maybe even ripped open in spots. There’s heavy marking in a few places, and it’s pretty clear some of the hull plating or fittings got displaced or damaged. But all we have are these images; they don’t tell us when or where they were taken.
These pictures started popping up after reports claimed that the PNS Hunain, a Pakistani offshore patrol vessel, collided with an Indian Navy warship in international waters on September 15. According to Indian sources quoted in several media outlets, the Pakistani ship did sustain damage and went back to port, while the Indian warship carried on with its mission. Indian media have mentioned a big dent and possible structural problems on the PNS Hunain, saying it had to return to harbor for repairs. Still, we don’t really know exactly how bad the damage is—there’s been no official word on whether there’s harm to deeper structural parts, internal spaces, or systems like propulsion.
If anyone can verify the source of these new photos, they might shed a bit more light on what really happened. But for now, it’s too early to say for sure that the damage shown comes from the September 15 collision. The images do show a ship with clear damage to its hull, but they don’t reveal how, when, or where it happened. Until we see more—things like extra photos, video, geolocation info, or official confirmation—these pictures remain unverified claims, not solid evidence of the incident.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

morning.title: India Must Protect Its “Apex Predator” From Becoming Strategic Vulnerabilities
morning.text:
It has shown through modern warfare that having an advanced combat platform is only one aspect of attaining battlefield superiority; the greater challenge lies in making sure that the platform stays survivable, operationally relevant and available throughout the conflict. For India, this lesson is especially significant when it comes to aircraft that have been described as the “apex predators” of the combat fleet, since such platforms involve a disproportionate amount of investment in technology, training and operational capability, and their being neutralised can give an adversary a psychological and informational victory even if the overall military campaign does not turn in its favour.
India must therefore reconsider the way in which it employs its most valuable combat aircraft. The aim should not merely be to use its most capable aircraft in a more aggressive manner, but rather to make sure that the enemy is never given an simple chance to concentrate its intelligence, surveillance and targeting resources on them. When an adversary has identified a specific aircraft type as the one that is most valuable, all the sensors, electronic-intelligence platforms, fighter patrols, long-range missiles and air-defence systems available to it will tend to be focused on locating and engaging that type.
This sets up a significant paradox: the more successful and technologically advanced an aircraft is, the greater its value as a target for an enemy. India has to make sure that its most capable fighter does not become predictable, and as a result, mission planning, route selection, the use of electronic warfare, decoys, escort fighters, support from airborne early-warning aircraft and dynamic targeting will become all the more important in protecting these aircraft.
Survivability must also be viewed as a capability at the system level and not merely as a feature of the aircraft by itself. A highly capable fighter can still become vulnerable should its supporting network be compromised. An aircraft operating with insufficient situational awareness, having only limited electronic-warfare support or following predictable mission patterns can be exposed even if it is equipped with good onboard sensors and weapons.
India should therefore create a multi-layered system surrounding its most valuable fighters, with airborne early-warning planes giving continuous situational awareness, electronic-warfare equipment making it difficult for the enemy to target them, unmanned systems being employed for reconnaissance and deception, and long-range weapons enabling the fighter to carry out its engagements without having to unnecessarily enter the most hazardous parts of the battlespace.
A vital lesson is that India should make sure that a single platform does not become indispensable. It is necessary to have a sufficient quantity of advanced fighters so that the loss or temporary withdrawal of any individual aircraft does not result in a severe operational effect. A technologically superior fighter operating as part of a large and resilient combat network is much harder to defeat than a small number of very valuable aircraft which have to carry an excessive portion of the mission load.
There is also a psychological aspect to this situation. Even if the actual military result is unchanged, the loss of a prominent combat platform can be turned into an opportunity in the field of information warfare by an opponent. They can make use of images, fragments, statements alleging a successful shot and the narratives that appear on social media to produce the impression that the whole weapons system has been beaten. India should therefore take this aspect into account and make sure that its operational planning and strategic communications avoid individual events on the battlefield being turned into an overestimated view of its overall combat capability.
The solution is not to keep India’s most capable fighters away from dangerous missions since an apex predator which is never given the opportunity to hunt offers little benefit; rather, India should make the platform hard to detect, hard to target and hard to destroy, and at the same time make use of its advanced sensors, weapons and networking capabilities to impose heavy costs on the adversary.
The main takeaway is that India’s most advanced fighter should not be regarded as just another item in its aircraft inventory; instead it symbolises a strategic capability for the purpose of which a complete combat ecosystem has to be developed. Since every conflict will cause the enemy to analyse India’s most sophisticated aircraft and to devise specific methods for countering them, India has to remain ahead of that process.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

morning.title: Southern Army Commander Reviews HAPS Program
morning.text:
Lt Gen Rajesh Pushkar, Army Commander, Southern Command, visited military establishments in Bengaluru, to review operational effectiveness, logistics preparedness, training standards, administration and welfare, with particular attention to emerging unmanned and counter-unmanned technologies.
During the visit, Lt Gen Pushkar was able to review preparedness of formations and establishments and interact with personnel in the domain of operational and support functions. The visit is at a time the Indian Army is focusing on unmanned systems, counter-drone capabilities and technology driven battlefield operations. At Headquarters Karnataka & Kerala Sub Area (KKSA) the Army Commander has looked into operational and administrative preparedness and also reviewed welfare initiatives for veterans and Veer Naris.
According to the information released about the visit, Lt Gen Pushkar appreciated the sustained efforts which the formation has taken up in these areas. The review covered both military and administrative aspects, indicating a diverse scope of work which falls under the responsibility of the Sub Area. One of the highlights of the Bengaluru visit was Lt Gen Pushkar’s visit to NewSpace Research & Technologies where he was able to witness drones and counter-drone systems being developed by the Bengaluru based defence technology company.
The systems displayed, are two growingly important elements of modern battlefield operations, unmanned aerial systems for surveillance and other missions and counter-UAS technologies to detect, track and counter hostile drones.
The Army has been upgrading its focus on capabilities such as these where the rapid proliferation of small drones, in modern conflicts, has presented a new challenge to armed forces. Their relative affordability, availability and the advantage to provide persistent aerial observation, make these systems a growing consideration for military planners. Lt Gen Pushkar praised the contributions made by NewSpace Research & Technologies towards Atmanirbharta in defence technology.
Bengaluru has become a critical node in India’s private-sector defence and aerospace ecosystem, with several companies focussing on unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronics and autonomous technologies. The visit reflects a growing interest in technology development in addition to conventional operational preparedness. However, the Army has not yet disclosed whether any of the systems demonstrated by NewSpace Research & Technologies have been formally trialed, evaluated by procurement agencies or inducted into service.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

morning.title: Tata Trusts v Tata Sons: Noel gets Singhvi on board
How Windows turned months of inactivity into a 7-hour update hostage situation
morning.text: Microsoft has a problem not entirely of its own making: The time it takes to bring a system back up to date after a few months of slumber. The company is keen to talk up how efficient it plans to make Windows. Not a day goes by without either a Microsoft representative or a fan insisting that Windows 11 is a lot snappier now than it used to be. (Usually they skirt the unfortunate truth that the Windows of yesteryear generally flies on modern hardware compared with the lumbering of today's software). Microsoft recently claimed that it is working to shrink Windows' footprint to the point where 8 GB would be enough to run things acceptably. We can only hope that one shard of light piercing the gloom of today's memory shortages and rising prices is that developers might prioritize efficient RAM use alongside slinging more ads or adding features few users require. However, this vulture's experience this week indicates that there is another area that needs addressing, and that is the number of updates slung out by vendors, and not just Microsoft. A few days ago, I wrote a story about a new way to skip the Microsoft account requirement during setup for the Home edition of Windows 11. At The Register, we like to test these claims thoroughly, so I fired up an x64 Windows laptop to check them out on real hardware, which is where the problems began. We've written before about the curse of updates, but this machine was running Windows 11 and had been up to date less than a year ago. How long could it take to get to the point where it would boot without Windows Update bleating about missed patches? The answer: about seven hours. Along with the huge array of updates for Windows components and the inevitable insistence that a new version of Microsoft's flagship operating system was needed, there were multiple firmware and driver updates and plenty of restarts. And, of course, there was the progress bar of lies and the percentage counter of deceit. In the decades since Microsoft first inflicted progress bars on Windows users, it has singularly failed to make them accurately reflect the, er, progress. "Yeah, so I'm going to stick at 65 percent for about an hour and then jump to 98 percent in 30 seconds before hanging there for another hour. Lol." That this behavior has endured for decades is beyond disappointing. Redmond is far from the only offender, but Windows' ubiquity makes it one of the most visible. To be clear, this was an ordinary Windows device, running a production version of the operating system. It just hadn't been turned on for a few months. The experience highlights a challenge Microsoft and its vendors must address. It's great that, at long last, people are considering code efficiency rather than simply flinging more hardware at badly written applications to make them run acceptably. But attention must also be paid to the constant flow of updates that seem to stem from an "ah well, we can always fix it in production" attitude that pervades the tech industry. Several years ago, the chief of a DevOps project was baffled when I asked him about testing and validation before release. Surely unit testing was sufficient? And the joy of modern development practices meant that if problems arose, an update could be swiftly rolled out. All of which assumes customers will tolerate continual updates, and a potential hours-long wait if, for some reason, they give it a few months between updates. The tech industry is waking up to the need for efficiencies, or at the very least Microsoft is. It also needs to deal with the scourge of update tsunamis. It's all well and good to brag about making your software run on limited resources until an interminable wait undermines the boast while the various widgets and components of a device insist on spending hours giving themselves a thorough update. Shaving a few seconds off the startup time means nothing if there are pages of updates awaiting the unwary. ®
